motion: American Democracy is in the worst crisis in a generation and Donald Trump is to blame.

dropped_turns.text: If democracy is larger than one leader, why excuse the leader's unique power to turn a lost election into a loyalty test? Can you name a stronger threat this generation has faced?

dropped_turns.speaker: CON

turns.text: Consider a local election worker who receives angry messages, reports them, and still helps count votes under established rules. The system offers remedies and the count proceeds. That proves resilience, not worst crisis.

turns.speaker: PRO

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Fear around counting is wrong, but you have not shown it came solely from Donald Trump or that it makes this the worst crisis. Institutions protect workers, investigate threats, and preserve voting despite politics.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When a president uses office to pressure officials to reverse a certified result, the crisis becomes acute. Donald Trump did that, so this is not ordinary polarization; it is an attack on consent.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your condition proves misconduct, not the sweeping resolution. An acute moment can be contained by lawful refusal, which happened. Calling every attack on consent the worst crisis erases differences in scale and endurance.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Democracy depends on a public willingness to accept legitimate losses, not only on officials refusing illegal demands. Donald Trump has weakened that willingness nationwide, making the crisis broader than one pressured certification.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: After a disputed count, neighbors can attend a public review, hear objections answered, and watch the final certification proceed. That process channels anger into rules rather than violence. It proves democratic repair remains available.
